title: When Algorithms Prescribe: A Cross-Sectional Study of Quality, Misinformation, and Engagement in Statin-Related Content on TikTok
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 258 English-language statin-related TikTok videos (scraped 14 November 2025 from 1,349 retrieved). Potential false claims flagged by two reviewers were independently adjudicated by two cardiology fellows against clinical evidence and classified true/false; a video counted as containing false claims if it carried at least one. The paper reports 102/258 (39.5%) of videos contained at least one false or misleading claim - a CONTENT share with an explicit denominator and an external expert ground truth. The paper also scores every video on DISCERN, PEMAT-AV and GQS, which are QUALITY instruments and are recorded as QUALITY rows excluded from prevalence.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two trained reviewers independently coded every video and flagged potential false or misleading claims, resolving discrepancies by discussion with a third reviewer as adjudicator; flagged claims were then independently reviewed by two subject-matter experts (both cardiology fellows) and classified true or false, with expert disagreements resolved by consensus. Quality-instrument inter-rater reliability was reported (ICC 0.808-0.906; Pearson r 0.814-0.907, all p < 0.001), but no separate kappa or ICC is reported for the false-claim classification itself.
estimates.moderator_quote: Potential claims were then independently reviewed by two subject matter experts, both cardiology fellows, and classified as true or false. Claims that were partially true, misleading, or lacking important clinical context were classified as false for the purposes of analysis.
estimates.notes: denom_selection = curated because the Apify scraper 'systematically retrieves the top-viewed publicly available videos corresponding to the specified search terms', i.e. a rank-truncated most-viewed set, not a random or census sample of statin videos. breadth = misleading (not 'false') because the coding rule explicitly folded partially-true claims and claims 'lacking important clinical context' into the false category, which is a lenient numerator. The 39.5% is the only whole-corpus prevalence figure; creator-type figures in Table 5 are subgroups of this same 258-video denominator (see missed_or_uncertain).

missed_or_uncertain: 1) CREATOR-TYPE BREAKDOWN OF FALSE CLAIMS (Table 5) was deliberately NOT split into rows: creator type is neither country, platform nor measure, so the splitting rule does not license sub-rows, and these five figures share the same 258-video denominator as the main row, so pooling them alongside it would double-count. Recorded here in full for the adjudicator: Physician 17/67 = 25.40% within group (16.67% of all false-claim videos); Non-physician healthcare provider 19/89 = 21.30% (18.63%); CAM health professionals 20/22 = 90.90% (19.61%); Wellness promoter 27/33 = 81.80% (26.47%); Layperson 19/47 = 40.40% (18.63%); Total 102/258 = 39.50%. Pearson chi-square(4, N = 258) = 66.92, p < 0.001, Cramer's V = 0.51. If the review wants a source-type moderator, these are the numbers to use. 2) TABLE 6 (categories of the 224 individual false claims) was not extracted as rows: those percentages are computed inside the misinformation-only set of claims (within_misinfo_content territory, R3) and there are 13 of them, which R4 argues against. Verbatim: statins significantly lower CoQ10 26 (11.61%); statins reduce cholesterol needed for hormone production 18 (8.04%); Alternatives 14 (6.25%); increased LDL doesn't cause heart disease 14 (6.25%); statins increase dementia risk 13 (5.80%); high cholesterol is not bad for health 13 (5.80%); statins cause significant muscle damage 9 (4.02%); statins don't prevent heart attack or stroke 9 (4.02%); statins reduce cholesterol in the brain 8 (3.57%); statins cause significant liver damage 7 (3.13%); statins deplete vitamin D 6 (2.68%); statins cause mood changes or depression 5 (2.23%); Miscellaneous 82 (36.61%); Total 224 (100%). Note the denominator here is 224 claims, not 258 videos. 3) NOT extracted because they are not misinformation shares: overall attitude toward statins (positive 60/23.3%, neutral 114/44.2%, negative 84/32.6%) is sentiment, not veracity; 'Misinformation and controversy' as a video TOPIC (22, 8.5%) counts videos that DISCUSS misinformation, not videos that contain it - an easy trap; thematic content shares (risks 63.2%, benefits 42.2%, mechanism 30.6%) and specific effect mentions (muscle pain 45.0%, cognitive changes 22.1%, etc.); creator-type composition (non-physician HCP 34.5%, physician 26.0%, layperson 18.2%, wellness promoter 12.8%, CAM 8.5%); video category (educational 91.09%, anecdotal 5.43%, entertainment 3.10%, other 0.39%); search-term composition of the included set (general terms 44.6%, atorvastatin 9.7%, simvastatin 8.5%, Zocor 1.9%, Crestor 0.8%, Pravachol 0.8%). 4) NO CONCENTRATION row: views are heavily right-skewed (range 101 to 2,100,000; mean 90,074 vs median 16,850; shares mean 1,029 vs median 42), but the paper never states a top-X%-of-videos-accounted-for-Y%-of-views figure, so R1 is not satisfied. 5) PEMAT-AV scores are a further QUALITY instrument but measure understandability and actionability (presentation), not accuracy, so no row was created: Understandability REV 1 63.0% (SD 21.0%) / REV 2 63.0% (SD 20.0%), ICC 0.848; Actionability REV 1 46.0% (SD 38.0%) / REV 2 50.0% (SD 38.0%), ICC 0.874. 6) COUNTRY is genuinely unresolved: the paper never states a geography. Coded Global because only an English-language filter was applied; a defensible alternative is United States, since the search terms were built from the most-prescribed US statins and the study is US-based. 7) This is a medRxiv preprint (posted 8 June 2026) not certified by peer review.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Data collected 14 November 2025 via an automated Apify scraper retrieving the top-viewed public TikTok videos for 15 predefined statin search terms (generic and brand names, singular and plural); 1,349 unique videos retrieved, 1,091 excluded on manual review (non-English, off-topic), 258 included. Two authors independently screened for eligibility with a third resolving discrepancies. Two blinded reviewers independently scored every video on DISCERN, PEMAT-AV and GQS; inter-rater reliability reported as ICC(2,1) 0.808-0.906, Pearson r 0.814-0.907 (all p < 0.001), with small but significant reviewer differences on PEMAT-Actionability (p = 0.002) and GQS (p = 0.001). Potential false or misleading claims were flagged by reviewers (discrepancies resolved by discussion, third-reviewer adjudication) and then independently adjudicated by two cardiology fellows, disagreements resolved by consensus; no reliability statistic is reported for the falsity classification itself. Analysis in SPSS 31, alpha 0.05; Welch's ANOVA with Games-Howell post hoc for quality by creator type; Pearson chi-square with Cramer's V for false claims by creator type. Key limitations for risk of bias: no probability sample (top-viewed algorithmic retrieval), English-only, no sampling weights, single scraping day, IRB-exempt public-data study, and a lenient falsity rule that folds partially-true and context-lacking claims into 'false'.

rob.item10_quote: Of 1,349 screened videos, 258 met inclusion criteria... and 39.5% contained at least one false or misleading claim, most often from complementary and alternative medicine providers and wellness promoters.
